subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Find the value of p, if the straight lines x+p=0, y+2=0, 3x+2y+5=0 are concurrent.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say why the first two lines need no solving, and what concurrency gives you.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Find the point of intersection
steps.margin_note: First mark. Two of the three lines are very simple — one fixes x, the other fixes y — so their meeting point can be written down without any solving.
steps.memory_tip: Two of the lines are very simple — one fixes x, the other y — so the point needs no solving.

recall.must_convey: That x = −p and y = −2 give the point of intersection (−p, −2).
accept: x plus p is zero so x is minus p and y is minus two

steps.why: A line of the form x + p = 0 is vertical and one of the form y + 2 = 0 is horizontal, so they cross at exactly one point that needs no algebra.
common_mistakes: Treating x + p = 0 as a line in both variables and trying to solve a system.
Reading x = p instead of x = −p.

steps.label: Substitute into the third line
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Concurrency puts that point on the third line as well, and the resulting equation has only p in it.
steps.memory_tip: Concurrency puts that point on the third line, and the equation has only p in it.
lines: But (−p, −2) lies on 3x + 2y + 5 = 0  [∵ Given lines are concurrent]

steps.why: Concurrency is the only condition given, and this substitution is the only place it can be used.
common_mistakes: Substituting into one of the first two lines.

insider_note: x + p = 0 and y + 2 = 0 each fix one coordinate, so the meeting point (−p, −2) reads straight off with no simultaneous equations. Substitute it into the THIRD line, not into one of the first two.
